30.0.0.en: David and his men returned and discovered that the Amalekites had taken advantage of his going out to the war and had raided the whole region of the South, including "Ziklag," in revenge on David, who had raided their land before (ch. 27). They also burned the city and took the women in it, as well as the remaining men and the children. They did not kill anyone, but took them as captives and slaves.

30.1.0.en: When David entered the town, they were shocked at what they saw of fire and destruction, and at its emptiness of women and sons, and they learned what had happened. So they cried out and wept, moved by what they saw, and their weeping went on until they had no strength left in them.

30.2.0.en: Both Ahinoam the Jezreelitess and Abigail, whom David married after the death of her husband Nabal, were also taken captive among the women who were taken captive.

30.3.0.en: David was greatly distressed by this calamity, and what doubled his distress and grief also was that the men, in their despair and frustration, turned against him and wanted to kill him, believing that he was the cause of everything that had come upon their wives and upon this city which he had left unguarded, and they counted that as negligence on his part. But David laid all his distress and pain before God, and felt His presence beside him, and his soul was strengthened and made strong.

30.3.1.en: We see that David here was in a severe predicament such as he had not met before, for the following reasons:

30.3.2.en: 1- He was pursued by Saul, who was trying to kill him, that is, he was driven out of his homeland.

30.3.3.en: 2- He was also rejected by the Philistines, because they refused his taking part with them in the war.

30.3.4.en: 3- He lost his wives and sons.

30.3.5.en: 4- His tents and possessions in Ziklag were burned.

30.3.6.en: 5- His men rose against him and tried to kill him, because he was accused of negligence in protecting their wives and children.

30.3.7.en: If loved ones and friends turn against you, take refuge in God, who is sure in His love and steadfast in His fatherhood, for He never changes. He will support you, and you will be able to win back many of those who turned against you.

30.4.0.en: Abiathar was the priest who escaped after Saul killed all the priests (ch. 22), and he had fled to David, taking with him the ephod and the stones of the Urim and Thummim. So David called for him and asked God through him whether he should pursue these Amalekite aggressors and whether he would have victory if he overtook them. God's answer came to him that he would prevail and would rescue the captives, the women and children. This was a good act on David's part, since he asked God and did not let his anger and desire for revenge lead him, and in this he learned from the earlier experience when he took refuge in Gath without asking God. We note here that when he prayed, God blessed him and his men submitted to him.

30.4.1.en: We also learn here not to be troubled by trials if we take refuge in God, because the trial turns into God's testing and the recovery of everything that was lost, and even the gaining of spoil. This is what happened with David, and it happens in our lives also, when we receive blessings from any trial.

30.5.0.en: The brook Besor: a depression south of Ziklag through which a stream, that is, a small river, runs from the mountains of Edom and empties into the Mediterranean Sea at Gaza, and perhaps it is what is called the river of Egypt, located on Egypt's border.

30.5.1.en: David took all his men, and when they reached the edge of the brook Besor, exhaustion and weariness overcame two hundred of his men and they could not go on. So David left them and continued on his way and crossed the brook with four hundred men.

30.5.2.en: Be gentle with people's abilities, and do not ask of them what is beyond their strength or make them feel at fault if they are worn out, for compassion and sensitivity to others are among the characteristics of the Christian!!

30.6.0.en: God sent new help to David by means of a guide who would help him reach the Amalekites. This help was an Egyptian man overcome by exhaustion and close to death, whom David's men found lying in a field, and they gave him food and drink, and when he had eaten he recovered some of his strength, for it was three days since he had eaten or drunk. This shows David's love and concern for the weak, for he helped this man who was at the point of death before he knew that he would be the one to guide him, and he did this despite his preoccupation with pursuing the invaders.

30.7.0.en: It appeared from the man's features and clothing that he was a slave and not from the people of this region, so David asked him whose man he was, "his master," and about his original homeland. The man answered him that he was a slave from Egypt and his master was an Amalekite, but he had fallen sick and his master had cruelly left him behind to meet his fate of death in this place?!!

30.8.0.en: The Cherethites: a people from the island of Crete who migrated east to the Philistine lands and merged with its people.

30.8.1.en: The man continued his speech, explaining the cause of his exhaustion and weariness, which was that he had taken part with the Amalekites, as a slave of his master, in invading the southern lands of the Cherethites, as well as the southern fields of Judah and the south of the lands of Caleb, and that they had also attacked Ziklag and burned it with fire.

30.9.0.en: David asked the man to guide him to the place of the Amalekites and their gathering, and the man, fearing for his life, asked David for an oath that he would not kill him or deliver him into the hands of his master, and David promised him this. So the man took him to the place where the Amalekites were gathered, who were celebrating with eating, drinking, dancing, and drunkenness after their victory over the land of the Philistines and Judah, for they thought David, the Philistines, and the Jews were occupied with war.

30.10.0.en: David waited until night, and after the Amalekites had gone to sleep, he and his men attacked them and kept fighting them fiercely throughout the night and the morning of the next day until its evening, and none of the Amalekites escaped except a small number of men, four hundred in all, who were able to flee on their camels. As for David, he was able to recover his two wives and all the spoil, of which nothing was lost, and he returned with all the sheep and the captives he drove before him, and everyone cried out that this was David's spoil. We note that those who cheered David were the very ones who had called for his death a little while before, so we should learn not to rely on people for anything, for they are changeable, moved by contradictory feelings, whereas reliance on God is the true refuge of the spiritual man.

30.11.0.en: David returned to the brook Besor, where he had left the two hundred exhausted men, and they came out to meet him after his victory. It was a kind gesture from David to ask about them and be reassured about their health, and he did not blame them for not going with him, since he recognized their physical weakness and their inability to continue the march with him.

30.12.0.en: Greed took hold of some of David's men, and they thought of the spoil more than their brothers did, so they spoke to David, saying to him that these men had not gone out with us to the war, and therefore it was enough for each of them to take his wife and children, and he should have no share of the spoil. The inspired text described everyone who thought thus as wicked and base.

30.13.0.en: David's answer, however, was wise. He spoke first about God's work among them and how it was God who gave them the victory and the material gifts, and also kept them from all harm and brought them back safe, so the victory and the good came from God and not from them. For this reason David denounced what they had said, and set a new rule which the generations after him took up: that he who guards the baggage and does not go down to the field of battle with the rest of the men shall have an equal share of the spoil with him who took part in the fighting, for his work was also important in preserving the supplies, and his poor health may be what kept him from fighting, so it is no fault of his that he should be deprived of his share. This agrees with God's Law that he who guards the baggage takes a share like him who fought (Num 31:

30.13.1.en: 25-27), although the men who did not fight were left behind because of their exhaustion and there was no baggage for them to guard, but he counted them like the one who guards the baggage and made allowance for them because of their exhaustion.

30.13.2.en: And David's wisdom in distributing the spoil to the fighters and also to those who did not take part because of their exhaustion kept the men from division.

30.14.0.en: David returned after his war to Ziklag, and after settling there he did not forget his friends from his true people, so he took a part of the spoil and sent it to them as an expression of his love for them, and as proof to them that his dwelling in the land of the Philistines had not affected him or put him outside his people. And when he sent these gifts he told them they were a blessing, that is, that he had no credit in them but they were a divine gift, which shows how humble David was and that he always ascribes the credit to God.

30.14.1.en: May we learn from David's virtues. First he had compassion on those whom exhaustion had overtaken and kept their share for them, and now too he sends gifts to his people, keeping himself clear of any greed, and when he gave the gifts he did not give them with a haughty heart but in a way in which he completely denied himself and ascribed the glory and the blessing to God.

30.15.0.en: In these verses the inspired text mentions for us the cities to which David sent the gifts, and they are:

30.15.1.en: 1- Bethel: it lies south of the lands of the tribe of Judah and is different from the famous Bethel that lies in the lands of the tribe of Benjamin. The word Bethel means the house of God, so it signifies God's receiving first from the spoil.

30.15.2.en: 2- Ramoth of the south: it lies in the lands of the tribe of Simeon.

30.15.3.en: 3- Jattir: it was one of the cities of refuge and lies in the mountains of Judea, about 21 km south of Hebron (Josh 15:48).

30.15.4.en: 4- Aroer: south of Beersheba, in the south of the lands of Israel.

30.15.5.en: 5- Siphmoth: one of the cities of southern Judah.

30.15.6.en: 6- Eshtemoa: also called Eshtemoh, about 17 km south of Hebron.

30.15.7.en: 7- Rachal: also one of the cities of Judah.

30.15.8.en: 8- The cities of the Kenites: they are the descendants of Jethro, the father-in-law of Moses.

30.15.10.en: 10- Chorashan: it was part of the lands of Judah and became Simeon's.

30.15.12.en: 12- Hebron: it is the present city of Hebron (al-Khalil).

30.15.13.en: The distribution of gifts also included all the places and towns where David and his men had wandered and whose people had hosted or supported them.

30.15.14.en: Be generous with others and do not forget kindness, and consider that the good which God has given you is good for you and for making others around you happy, for the more you give, the more God gives you an increase of His goodness and fills your heart with every joy.

30.15.15.en: The defeat of Israel and the end of Saul

31.0.s.en: (1) The defeat of Israel and the killing of Saul and his sons

31.0.0.en: The war began, and because of the great numbers of the Philistines, the men of Israel fled before them and went back to Mount Gilboa (ch. 28:4) to catch their breath, but the Philistines followed them and struck down many dead. God permitted this because of the evil of Saul and his people.

31.1.0.en: Followed hard upon: they hastened with all their strength.

31.1.1.en: The Philistines' first aim was to seize Saul and his sons and kill them, so they strove for this with all their strength, until they were indeed able to kill his three sons: Jonathan, the dearest of friends to David's heart, and Abinadab and Malchishua. Nothing is mentioned here about Saul's fourth son, Ish-bosheth, who perhaps did not take part in the war.

31.1.2.en: And the death of the pure-hearted Jonathan resulted from the evil of his father Saul, for the Jews were defeated before the Philistines, but on the Day of Judgment Jonathan will be rewarded and will have a place in the Kingdom according to his righteousness.

31.1.3.en: And perhaps Jonathan's death rescued David from a predicament at his being crowned king over the children of Israel, because Jonathan was the heir apparent and David was the one anointed by God, and if Jonathan had renounced the kingship it would seem as if he had given the kingdom to David and not God.

31.2.0.en: Archers: those who shoot arrows by means of bows.

31.2.1.en: The Philistines continued to concentrate on Saul, and they rained arrows on him from every side until he was struck with a deep wound.

31.2.2.en: We note here that at the very time when David triumphs over the Amalekites, Saul is defeated before the Philistines, because he who walks with God is victorious, while he who is far from God is defeated.

31.3.0.en: The uncircumcised: that is, those not circumcised, meaning the Philistines.

31.3.1.en: Saul knew the end, and that his deep wound had no cure, so he asked his bodyguard and armor-bearer to hasten his death and to thrust him through the heart with the sword so that he would die quickly. And because this matter was of course hard for his armor-bearer, Saul explained to him that the Philistines would seize him and torture him and make a spectacle of his body, as they had done to Samson before when they put out his eyes and made him work like an animal pulling the mill in their temple (Judg 16:21, 25). And when Saul found his man very afraid, he took the sword and set its hilt on the ground with its sharp end pointing upward, and fell on it with the weight of his body, and the sword pierced him and he died. And so all of Saul's wicked plans came to nothing, he who had tried to kill David many times lest he seize the kingdom from Jonathan; but now Saul dies and sees with his own eyes the death of his three sons, and indeed his pursuit of David had kept David away from his homeland and consequently from this war, and so God preserved him to become king over Israel. So do not fear the plans of the wicked, for they are all in vain, and God brings about the opposite of them as long as you rely on Him.

31.4.0.en: And as Saul did, so also did his armor-bearer, as a kind of loyalty to his master, or perhaps from fear of the Philistines seizing him, and so was the end of Saul and his sons and the men around him.

31.5.0.en: The other side of the valley: what is meant is the valley of Jezreel.

31.5.1.en: As for the men who had not gone out to the war, whether they were on the other side of the valley or beyond the Jordan River, when the news reached them of Saul's death and the flight of the men of Israel, they too fled from their cities in fear, and the Philistines advanced and occupied them without the slightest resistance.

31.6.0.en: To strip the slain: something the victors do in order to take the clothes, weapons, and valuable possessions.

31.6.1.en: Beth-shan: about 8 km west of the Jordan.

31.6.2.en: As for the Philistines, their conduct was very savage, for when they searched among the corpses they found Saul and his sons among the slain, and they cut off his head from his body and took his spear and his sword, and sent messengers to the Philistine cities to announce the news of Saul's fall and killing, and to give thanks to the pagan gods in their temples. And as the Israelites had done before, placing Goliath's weapons in the tabernacle of meeting, so the Philistines placed Saul's weapons in the house of their most famous goddess, Ashtaroth, whose temple is in Ashkelon. This act meant their thanks to their gods who had given them victory.

31.6.3.en: And they were not satisfied with this, but in utmost savagery they also nailed his body to the wall of the town of Beth-shan as a form of gloating.

31.6.4.en: God permitted the killing of Saul and his sons in the war as a result of his sins and the sins of many of his people. So take heed to yourself and keep away from sin, which destroys its owner, and do not be dazzled by temporary successes and passing material things, but let your eyes be on your goal, which is eternity, and be patient in sufferings, and you will secure your peace in this life and your place in the Kingdom.

31.7.s.en: (2) The men of Jabesh bury Saul and his sons

31.7.0.en: The inhabitants of "Jabesh-gilead" were the ones whom Saul had earlier rescued from "Nahash," king of the Ammonites, who wanted to put out their eyes, and they had not forgotten what Saul did but kept their gratitude to him. So when they heard what the Philistines had done to Saul, they gathered all their valiant men, and at nightfall, when everyone was asleep, they crept to the wall of the city of Beth-shan and took the bodies of Saul and his three sons and burned them in their town when they returned. And perhaps the reason for their burning these bodies was so that the Philistines would not come back to take them and make a spectacle of them again, or to remove the shame that had come upon Saul's body after it was disfigured by the cutting off of his head.

31.8.0.en: The tamarisk tree: a kind of tree which apparently was well known in the city of Jabesh, and it became a monument and memorial of the burial place of Saul and his sons.

31.8.1.en: After the burning of the bodies the bones remained, and they buried them with the utmost respect under one of the well-known trees of the town, and fasted seven days in self-denial, in honor of the king, who bore the symbol of the whole people on the one hand, and for their special love of the person of Saul, who had rescued them before.

31.8.2.en: And so this book began with the birth of Samuel, the fruit of prayer, and ends with the death of Saul, who relied on his own strength, so that the book may confirm the importance of prayer and reliance on God.

31.8.3.en: ? So ended the life of the first of the kings of the children of Israel. Although God blessed him and anointed him king, and although he also began his life humble, he became arrogant and relied on himself, and killed the priests of the Most High God and disobeyed God's commands, so his end was a sad and harsh end, which he deserved because he did not remain as he was at first. Let us then beware of the end, for the wise man does not care how his beginning is but is always careful what his end will be!?!

31.8.4.en: The life of Saul - When the children of Israel asked Samuel for a king and he rebuked them for it, God afterward agreed and guided him to Saul the son of Kish, who was looking for his father's donkeys, and he anointed him king (chs. 9, 10). - Samuel gathered the people at Mizpeh and cast lots, and the lot fell on Saul, and he proclaimed him king among the people (ch. 10), and that was in the year 1079 B.C.

31.8.5.en: - Saul triumphed over Nahash, king of the Ammonites, and freed Jabesh-gilead, and Samuel renewed the kingship for him and the people's allegiance at Gilgal (ch. 11). - The Philistines prepared to attack the children of Israel, and when Samuel was late in coming to Saul, Saul offered the sacrifice in his place; then Samuel came and rebuked him and declared to him that God had rejected him and would raise up a good king in his place, but God gave him victory over the Philistines (chs. 13, 14). - He fought Amalek as the Lord commanded, but disobeyed Him in sparing Agag their king and the spoil, so Samuel rebuked him and killed Agag, and left Saul, who laid hold of his mantle so that it tore, and Samuel said to him that God would tear his kingdom (ch. 15). - An evil spirit came upon Saul, and they brought David to him to play the harp for him so that he would be calmed (ch. 16). - The Philistines prepared to fight the children of Israel, and Goliath reproached the people of God, and David killed him, and the women cheered and glorified David more than Saul, so Saul was enraged (ch. 18). - Saul asked David for a hundred foreskins of the Philistines as a dowry for his daughter, in order to be rid of him, and he brought him two hundred and married Michal.

31.8.6.en: - Saul tried to kill David and seize him several times, but he escaped with Jonathan's help and went to Nob, the city of the priests, and took Goliath's sword (chs. 18-21). - Saul went out to look for David to seize him and killed the priests, and David fled to many places and then to the Philistines at Gath (ch. 21). - Saul continued to pursue David, but he fell into David's hand twice, and David forgave him and let him go, the first time when David cut off the edge of his robe (ch. 24) and the second when he took his spear and his jug of water (ch. 26). - A new attack by the Philistines, and Saul went to ask the medium, and Samuel appeared to him and rebuked him and informed him that he would die in the war, he and his sons, and that indeed came to pass, and the Philistines hung his body and the bodies of his sons on the city wall, and the men of Jabesh-gilead took them down and burned them and buried them, and that was in the year 1055 B.C. (chs. 28-31).
